title: Thrombosis and thrombophilia
covers: The hemostatic balance and Virchow's triad, the coagulation factors and their natural inhibitors, inherited thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency), antiphospholipid syndrome, and when to test.

items.p: Hemostasis is a complex, highly regulated process of cellular and biochemical events. It keeps blood liquid inside vessels and stops blood loss after injury by forming a clot.
It is a balance of platelets, coagulation, fibrinolysis and the vessels. Tipping it one way gives thrombosis; the other way gives bleeding.

ul: Abnormal blood flow
Abnormal vessel wall
Abnormal blood: the hypercoagulable state

table: Coagulation system (plasma proteins, platelets) and fibrinolytic system (plasma proteins; platelets, endothelium)

items.p: Platelet aggregation (primary) and thrombin-made fibrin (secondary) run together and form the hemostatic clot over about 10 minutes.

ul: Extrinsic: factor VII + tissue factor → VIIa/TF, which activates X (and IX)
Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX; IXa with VIIIa, phospholipid and Ca²⁺ activates X
Xa with Va, phospholipid and Ca²⁺ turns prothrombin into thrombin
Thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin and activates XIII → stabilized fibrin clot

items.p: Mostly glycoproteins, mostly made in the liver (a few in monocytes, endothelium and megakaryocytes). Eight circulate as zymogens; four are cofactors. "a" means the active form. There is no factor VI. Platelet factor 3, prekallikrein and HMWK have no Roman numeral.
von Willebrand factor carries factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion. Platelet factor 3 is phosphatidylserine, an assembly molecule.

items.note: On slide 18 the colors in the "physical properties" legend (vitamin K-dependent, thrombin-sensitive, contact) do not match the colors in the table, and prekallikrein is listed at "35–50 µg/dL" (usual references: about 35–50 µg/mL). The groupings and concentrations (except fibrinogen) are not tested.

ul: Thrombomodulin and the endothelial protein C receptor activate protein C
Activated protein C, with protein S as its cofactor, inactivates Va and VIIIa. This controls thrombin generation.
Antithrombin (antithrombin III), with heparan sulfate, neutralizes thrombin
Antithrombin irreversibly binds thrombin (IIa), IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa. Heparin binds antithrombin, changes its shape and speeds the reaction about 1000-fold.

table: Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C or S deficiency
Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C and S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency
Surgery, trauma, immobility, prolonged travel, inflammation, malignancy, estrogens, antiphospholipid antibodies, HIT, myeloproliferative disease (JAK2+)
Hyperhomocysteinemia, PNH, acquired protein C resistance, high factor VIII, IX, XI
FVL, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiency

items.p: The most common inherited thrombophilia: 40–50% of inherited cases (prothrombin mutation 10–20%).

ul: First described in 1993 in Leiden, the Netherlands
Autosomal dominant; heterozygous disease is milder than homozygous; about 1% of carriers are homozygous
Usually venous, not arterial
A guanine-to-adenine point mutation: Arg506Gln (R506Q). Factor Va resists cleavage by activated protein C.
Other factor V variants: Cambridge Arg306Thr, Hong Kong Arg306Gly, Liverpool Ile359Thr

items.note: Slide 24 says "arginine substituted for glutamine", which reverses the change. Slides 22 and 36 give it correctly: arginine at 506 is replaced by glutamine (Arg506Gln). Only Arg506Gln is tested.

table: Relative risk of a first VTE

summary.h: Prothrombin G20210A, protein C and antithrombin

ul: Prothrombin G20210A: a G-to-A change at nucleotide 20210 (a factor II polymorphism) raises prothrombin levels by about 30%
Protein C deficiency: Va and VIIIa are no longer switched off
Antithrombin deficiency: thrombin and the other serine proteases are not neutralized; heparin works through antithrombin

items.note: For heterozygous G20210A, slide 26 gives a "3–6 fold" higher risk, while the table on slide 25 gives a relative risk of 2.8. Neither number is tested.

items.p: Prevalence among patients with venous thrombosis:

table: Antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiency

items.p: Primary, or secondary to lupus. Anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant antibodies are found in 1–5% of young, apparently healthy people.

ul: Thrombosis: one or more arterial, venous or small-vessel events, in any tissue or organ

Pregnancy: one or more unexplained deaths of a normal fetus at 10 weeks or later; or one or more premature births of a normal baby at or before 34 weeks from severe preeclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency; or three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks (anatomic, hormonal and chromosomal causes excluded)

items.p: Laboratory (each on two or more occasions at least 6 weeks apart):

ul: Anticardiolipin IgG and/or IgM in medium or high titer (standardized ELISA, β2-GPI–dependent)

Lupus anticoagulant: a prolonged phospholipid-dependent screening test (aPTT, kaolin clotting time, dilute Russell's viper venom time, dilute PT, Textarin time), no correction on mixing with normal plasma, shortening with excess phospholipid, and other causes excluded (factor VIII inhibitor, heparin)
aPTT normal → dRVVT; both normal → stop
Abnormal → mixing study. Fails to correct → test phospholipid dependence: positive = LA confirmed; negative → factor assays
Mix corrects → incubated mixing study: fails to correct → phospholipid dependence; corrects → factor assays (specific deficiency or inhibitor)

summary.h: When to test, and the cases

ul: Thrombosis at a young age
Clots in unusual locations
Repeated unprovoked events
Family history of venous or arterial clots at a young age

items.p: Lecturer's point: testing "is usually not the answer on your board".

Case 1 (slides 2–7): a 43-year-old woman with syncope. She had coronary stents at 31 and a PE in 2004, and smokes. Now she has bilateral DVTs, a PE and a cool foot with absent pulses: both arterial and venous clots, which points to lupus anticoagulant (or hyperhomocysteinemia) rather than FVL or the deficiencies.
Case 2 (slides 37–38): a 28-year-old woman with a DVT at 30 weeks of pregnancy after years of oral contraceptives. The clot has a clear trigger, so the best answer is no further testing.

items.note: The slides give no answer key for either case. The answers here are worked out from slides 34 and 39.

cards.q: Virchow's triad
cards.a: Abnormal blood flow, abnormal vessel wall, abnormal blood (hypercoagulable state)

cards.q: Primary versus secondary hemostasis
cards.a: Primary: vessels and platelets. Secondary: coagulation and fibrinolytic systems.

cards.q: Which complex converts prothrombin to thrombin?
cards.a: Xa with Va, phospholipid and Ca²⁺

cards.q: Which complex starts the extrinsic pathway?
cards.a: VIIa with tissue factor (activates X and IX)

cards.q: Which factor stabilizes the fibrin clot, and what kind of enzyme is it?
cards.a: XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor), a transglutaminase activated by thrombin

cards.q: Factor IX, X and XII common names
cards.a: IX Christmas; X Stuart–Prower; XII Hageman

cards.q: Labile versus stable factor
cards.a: Labile = V (cofactor); stable = VII (serine protease)

cards.q: Cofactors among the coagulation factors
cards.a: III (tissue factor), V, VIII, HMWK

cards.q: Factor numbers that do not exist or are not assigned
cards.a: There is no factor VI; PF3, prekallikrein and HMWK have no Roman numeral

cards.q: How is protein C activated, and what does it inactivate?
cards.a: By thrombomodulin (with the endothelial protein C receptor); with protein S it inactivates Va and VIIIa

cards.q: Factors irreversibly bound by antithrombin
cards.a: Thrombin (IIa), IXa, Xa, XIa, XIIa

cards.q: How does heparin act?
cards.a: Binds antithrombin, changes its shape, amplifies its action about 1000-fold

cards.q: Mechanism of FVL, G20210A, protein C/S deficiency versus antithrombin deficiency
cards.a: First group: decreased control of thrombin generation. Antithrombin deficiency: decreased neutralization of thrombin.

cards.q: Most common inherited thrombophilia
cards.a: Factor V Leiden (40–50% of inherited cases)

cards.q: Factor V Leiden: mutation and effect
cards.a: Arg506Gln (G→A point mutation); factor Va resists cleavage by activated protein C

cards.q: Factor V Leiden: inheritance and usual site
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (homozygotes worse); usually venous

cards.q: Relative risk of first VTE: FVL heterozygous, OCP, both, FVL homozygous
Prothrombin G20210A: what it is and its effect
cards.a: G→A change at nucleotide 20210; prothrombin levels about 30% higher

cards.q: Thrombophilias that cause arterial and venous thrombosis
cards.a: Hyperhomocysteinemia and lupus anticoagulant

cards.q: Thrombophilias that cause venous thrombosis only
cards.a: FVL, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C and protein S deficiency

cards.q: Acquired thrombophilias (slide 17)
cards.a: Surgery, trauma, immobility, prolonged travel, inflammation, malignancy, estrogens, antiphospholipid antibodies, HIT, MPD (JAK2+)

cards.q: "Others/mixed" causes of thrombosis
cards.a: Hyperhomocysteinemia, PNH, acquired protein C resistance, high factor VIII, IX, XI

cards.q: Antiphospholipid syndrome: diagnosis rule
cards.a: 1 clinical criterion + 1 laboratory criterion (Sapporo)

cards.q: APS pregnancy criteria: three timings
cards.a: Fetal death at ≥ 10 weeks; premature birth at ≤ 34 weeks (preeclampsia, placental insufficiency); ≥ 3 consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks

cards.q: APS lab criteria: repeat interval (Sapporo 1998)
cards.a: Positive on two or more occasions at least 6 weeks apart

cards.q: Lupus anticoagulant: mixing and phospholipid results
cards.a: Does not correct on mixing; shortens with excess phospholipid

cards.q: Indications for a thrombophilia work-up
cards.a: Young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of clots at a young age

questions.stem: Hemostasis keeps blood liquid inside the vessels. What is its other main role?

options.A: Removing damaged red cells from the circulation
options.B: Forming clots that stop bleeding after injury
options.C: Clearing immune complexes from the plasma
options.D: Carrying oxygen signals to the marrow
options.E: Recycling iron from senescent red cells

questions.explanation: Hemostasis is a complex, regulated process of cellular and biochemical events that keeps blood liquid in the vessels and prevents blood loss after injury through clot formation. A: The spleen does that. C: Not a role of hemostasis. D: Not a role of hemostasis. E: Macrophages do that.

questions.stem: Overactivity of which component pushes the hemostatic balance toward bleeding?
questions.explanation: Hemostasis balances platelets, coagulation, fibrinolysis and the vessels. Too much fibrinolysis tips it toward bleeding. A: Pushes toward thrombosis. B: Pushes toward thrombosis. C: Pushes toward thrombosis. D: Pushes toward thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man, bedbound for three weeks after a stroke, develops a DVT. Which arm of Virchow's triad does his immobility represent?
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad: abnormal blood flow (stasis), abnormal vessel wall, abnormal blood (the hypercoagulable state). B: Immobility slows flow; it does not damage the wall. C: The hypercoagulable state. D: Not an arm of the triad. E: Not an arm of the triad.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with factor V Leiden has a DVT. Which arm of Virchow's triad does her mutation represent?
questions.explanation: A thrombophilia is a change in the blood itself: the hypercoagulable state, the third arm of Virchow's triad. A: Stasis, e.g. immobility. B: Endothelial injury. C: Not an arm of the triad. E: Not an arm of the triad.

questions.stem: A patient with a platelet function defect bleeds after a dental extraction. Which part of hemostasis is defective?
questions.explanation: Primary hemostasis: the vascular system (endothelium, subendothelium/collagen) and platelets. Secondary: the coagulation and fibrinolytic systems. A: Plasma proteins (secondary). B: Secondary hemostasis. D: Part of coagulation. E: Natural anticoagulant.

questions.stem: Besides plasma proteins and platelets, which cells take part in the fibrinolytic system?
questions.explanation: Fibrinolytic system: plasma proteins; cells: platelets and endothelium. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. E: Make factors, but not listed as fibrinolytic cells.

questions.stem: What does secondary hemostasis add to the platelet aggregate to form the hemostatic clot?
questions.explanation: Primary: platelet aggregation. Secondary: coagulation, thrombin → fibrin. Together they make the hemostatic clot over about 10 minutes. B: Fibrinolysis. C: Primary hemostasis. D: Adhesion, primary hemostasis. E: Anticoagulant.

questions.stem: Tissue factor binds which factor to start the extrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic: factor VII + tissue factor → VIIa/TF, which activates X and IX. A: Activated by VIIa/TF. B: Starts the intrinsic pathway. D: Intrinsic pathway. E: Activated by VIIa/TF.

questions.stem: Which factor activates factor IX in the intrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic: XII → XIIa → XI → XIa → IX → IXa. A: Activates XI. C: A cofactor of IXa. D: Downstream of IXa. E: Not the activator of IX shown.

questions.stem: Factor IXa needs which cofactor to activate factor X?
questions.explanation: IXa with VIIIa, phospholipid and Ca²⁺ activates X. A: The cofactor of Xa. B: The cofactor of VIIa. C: A contact cofactor. D: The cofactor of activated protein C.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts prothrombin to thrombin?
questions.explanation: Xa with Va, phospholipid and Ca²⁺ turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin. B: Activates X. C: Activates X and IX. D: Activates IX. E: Contact activation.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds late after surgery. His PT and aPTT are normal, but his fibrin clot is not cross-linked. Which factor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Thrombin activates XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor), which stabilizes the fibrin clot. A: Contact factor. B: Intrinsic pathway. D: Extrinsic pathway. E: Cofactor of Xa.

questions.stem: What kind of enzyme is factor XIII?
questions.explanation: Factor XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor) is a transglutaminase. A: VII, IX, X, XI, XII, prekallikrein. B: III, V, VIII, HMWK. C: Not listed. D: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which endothelial molecule activates protein C?
questions.explanation: Thrombomodulin, with the endothelial protein C receptor, activates protein C. A: Starts coagulation. B: Works with antithrombin. C: Carrier of VIII; adhesion. E: Cofactor of activated protein C.

questions.stem: Which protein is the cofactor of activated protein C?
questions.explanation: Activated protein C, with protein S, inactivates Va and VIIIa, controlling thrombin generation. A: Neutralizes thrombin. C: Activates protein C. D: Contact cofactor. E: Works with antithrombin.

questions.stem: Which complex neutralizes thrombin on the endothelium?
questions.explanation: Thrombin generation is controlled by the protein C pathway; thrombin itself is neutralized by the antithrombin–heparan sulfate complex. A: Inactivates Va and VIIIa. B: Activates protein C. C: Starts coagulation. D: Fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A patient's thrombophilia lets thrombin form at a normal rate but stops it from being neutralized. Which defect is it?
questions.explanation: FVL, G20210A and protein C or S deficiency → decreased control of thrombin generation. Antithrombin deficiency → decreased neutralization of thrombin. B: Less control of thrombin generation. C: Less control of thrombin generation. D: Less control of thrombin generation. E: Less control of thrombin generation.

questions.stem: Where are most coagulation factors synthesized?
questions.explanation: Coagulation factors are mostly glycoproteins made in the liver (a few in monocytes, endothelium and megakaryocytes); eight circulate as zymogens; four are cofactors. A: Makes a few. B: Make a few. C: Make a few. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factor number is not assigned?
questions.explanation: Factors carry Roman numerals ("a" = active). No factor VI is assigned; platelet factor 3, prekallikrein and HMWK have no Roman numeral. A: Ionized calcium. C: Tissue factor. D: Fibrin-stabilizing factor. E: Plasma thromboplastin antecedent.

questions.stem: Which clotting protein has a Roman numeral?
questions.explanation: Tissue factor is factor III. Prekallikrein, HMWK and platelet factor 3 have no Roman numerals. A: No numeral. B: No numeral. D: No numeral. E: No numeral.

questions.stem: Which factor acts as a cofactor rather than a serine protease?
questions.explanation: Cofactors: III, V, VIII, HMWK. Serine proteases: VII, IX, X, XI, XII, prekallikrein. XIII: transglutaminase. A: Serine protease. B: Serine protease. C: Serine protease. D: Serine protease.

questions.stem: Which factor is the Christmas factor?
questions.explanation: IX Christmas, X Stuart–Prower, XI plasma thromboplastin antecedent, XII Hageman, XIII fibrin-stabilizing. A: Stuart–Prower factor. B: Hageman factor. C: Plasma thromboplastin antecedent. E: Antihemophilic factor.

questions.stem: Which protein is the Fletcher factor?
questions.explanation: Prekallikrein = Fletcher factor (serine protease); HMWK = Fitzgerald factor (cofactor). A: Fitzgerald factor. C: Hageman factor. D: Plasma thromboplastin antecedent. E: Labile factor.

questions.stem: Which factor is known as the labile factor?
questions.explanation: V = labile factor (cofactor); VII = stable factor (serine protease). A: Stable factor. B: Antihemophilic factor. D: Stuart–Prower factor. E: Fibrin-stabilizing factor.

questions.stem: A patient has no von Willebrand factor in plasma. Which coagulation factor is also low?
questions.explanation: von Willebrand factor carries factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion. B: Not carried by vWF. C: Not carried by vWF. D: Not carried by vWF. E: Not carried by vWF.

questions.stem: Which molecule is platelet factor 3?
questions.explanation: Platelet factor 3 is phosphatidylserine, an assembly molecule. A: Not PF3. B: A different molecule. C: Not PF3. D: Factor III.

questions.stem: What is the normal plasma concentration of fibrinogen?
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen (factor I), the fibrin precursor: 200–400 mg/dL. A: Too low. B: Too high. C: Prothrombin. E: Factor V or X.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a hepatic vein thrombosis, a high hematocrit and platelet count, and a JAK2 mutation. Which other risk factor belongs to the same group as his?
questions.explanation: JAK2+ myeloproliferative disease is an acquired risk factor, with HIT, APL antibodies, estrogens, malignancy, inflammation, surgery, trauma, immobility and prolonged travel. A: Hereditary. B: Hereditary. D: Others/mixed. E: Others/mixed.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a DVT, DAT-negative hemolysis and red cells lacking CD55 and CD59. Which risk factor is grouped with her condition?
questions.explanation: PNH sits in the "others/mixed" group with hyperhomocysteinemia, acquired protein C resistance and high levels of factors VIII, IX and XI. B: Acquired. C: Acquired. D: Hereditary. E: Acquired.

questions.stem: Each is a hereditary thrombophilia EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hereditary: FVL, prothrombin mutation, protein C and S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency. Acquired protein C resistance is in the others/mixed group. A: Hereditary. C: Hereditary. D: Hereditary. E: Hereditary.

questions.stem: Which inherited thrombophilia accounts for 40–50% of inherited cases?
questions.explanation: FVL (40–50%) is the most common inherited thrombophilia; the prothrombin mutation follows (10–20%). A: 10–20%. B: Less common. D: Less common. E: Less common.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman of Dutch descent has a DVT, and her factor Va resists cleavage by activated protein C. How is her disorder inherited?
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden is autosomal dominant; heterozygous disease is less severe than homozygous. A: Not X-linked. B: Not X-linked. C: Not mitochondrial. E: Not Y-linked.

questions.stem: Which thrombosis does factor V Leiden usually cause?
questions.explanation: FVL usually causes venous thrombosis, as opposed to arterial. A: Arterial. B: Arterial. C: Arterial. D: Arterial.

questions.stem: When and where was factor V Leiden first described?
questions.explanation: First described in 1993 in Leiden, the Netherlands. B: 1993. C: Leiden is in the Netherlands. D: 1993, Leiden. E: 1993.

questions.stem: Which amino acid change defines factor V Leiden?
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden is R506Q (Arg506Gln). Cambridge Arg306Thr, Hong Kong Arg306Gly, Liverpool Ile359Thr. A: Factor V Cambridge. C: Factor V Hong Kong. D: Factor V Liverpool. E: The prothrombin gene mutation.

questions.stem: Which pair of factor V variants changes residue 306?
questions.explanation: Cambridge Arg306Thr and Hong Kong Arg306Gly. A: Leiden is at 506. B: Liverpool is at 359. C: 506 and 359. D: Liverpool is at 359.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a DVT has a guanine-to-adenine point mutation in his factor V gene. Which laboratory finding is expected?

options.B: Low protein C activity on assay

questions.explanation: The FVL mutation makes factor V resistant to cleavage by activated protein C. B: Protein C is normal. C: Antithrombin is normal. D: G20210A. E: Acquired antibody.

questions.stem: Roughly what share of people with the factor V Leiden mutation are homozygous?
questions.explanation: About 1% of people with the mutation are homozygous. A: About 1%. B: About 1%. C: About 1%. E: About 1%.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives is heterozygous for factor V Leiden. What is her relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Relative risk: FVL heterozygous 7, OCP 4, both 35 (0.29% per year), FVL homozygous 80. A: FVL heterozygous alone. B: OCP alone. D: The combined risk is far higher. E: FVL homozygous.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is homozygous for factor V Leiden. What is her yearly incidence of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: FVL homozygous: relative risk 80, 0.5–1.0% per year. A: FVL heterozygous. C: FVL heterozygous with OCP. D: Normal. E: OCP alone.

questions.stem: A man is heterozygous for factor V Leiden and takes no estrogen. What is his relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Heterozygous FVL: relative risk 7 (0.06% per year); homozygous 80. B: Hyperhomocysteinemia. C: Heterozygous with OCP. D: Homozygous. E: OCP alone.

questions.stem: Which of these carries the lowest relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Relative risks: hyperhomocysteinemia 2.5, OCP 4, FVL heterozygous 7, with OCP 35, homozygous 80. A: 4. B: 7. D: 35. E: 80.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a DVT. Her prothrombin level is about 30% above normal, and her factor V gene is normal. Which mutation is most likely?
questions.explanation: Prothrombin G20210A, a G-to-A change at nucleotide 20210, raises prothrombin levels by ~30%. A: Factor V gene normal. C: Factor V gene normal. D: Does not raise prothrombin. E: Does not raise prothrombin.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a DVT receives unfractionated heparin, but his aPTT barely changes even at high doses. Which inherited thrombophilia best explains this?
questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin and amplifies its action ~1000-fold; with too little antithrombin, heparin works poorly. A: Heparin acts through antithrombin. B: Heparin acts through antithrombin. C: Heparin acts through antithrombin. D: Heparin acts through antithrombin.

questions.stem: Which activated factor is NOT a target of antithrombin?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin irreversibly binds thrombin (IIa), IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa. Va is inactivated by activated protein C. A: Target. B: Target. C: Target. E: Target.

questions.stem: How does heparin enhance antithrombin?

options.A: It raises antithrombin synthesis in the liver
options.C: It activates protein C on endothelium
options.E: It binds and blocks tissue factor

questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin, changing its shape so it binds thrombin and other serine proteases more avidly (~1000-fold). A: It acts on the existing molecule. C: Thrombomodulin does that. D: Activated protein C does that. E: Not its action.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had two DVTs. Protein C activity is low; antithrombin and APC-resistance tests are normal. Which control step is lost?

options.A: Inactivation of factors IXa and Xa
options.D: Inactivation of factors Va and VIIIa

questions.explanation: Activated protein C, with protein S, inactivates Va and VIIIa. Protein C deficiency removes this control. A: Antithrombin targets. B: Antithrombin is normal. C: Not a control step. E: Not a control step.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus has a DVT and a persistent lupus anticoagulant. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: APS may be primary or secondary to lupus. Thrombosis plus a persistent lupus anticoagulant in lupus = secondary APS. A: No heparin exposure. B: Not suggested. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old blood donor has a positive anticardiolipin test once. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: It occurs in 1–5% of healthy people

questions.explanation: Anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant antibodies are found in 1–5% of young, apparently healthy people. B: Needs a clinical criterion and a repeat test. C: Not by itself. D: No clinical event. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: Which event meets the Sapporo vascular thrombosis criterion?

options.C: One small-vessel thrombosis in a kidney

questions.explanation: Clinical criterion 1: one or more episodes of arterial, venous or small-vessel thrombosis, in any tissue or organ. A: Not thrombosis of the listed vessels. B: Bleeding, not thrombosis. D: Not thrombosis. E: Not a listed criterion.

questions.stem: Which pregnancy history meets the Sapporo clinical criteria?

options.A: Delivery at 33 weeks for severe preeclampsia
options.B: Delivery at 36 weeks for severe preeclampsia
options.E: Three miscarriages with a septate uterus

questions.explanation: Pregnancy morbidity: ≥ 1 unexplained death of a normal fetus at ≥ 10 weeks; ≥ 1 premature birth at ≤ 34 weeks from severe preeclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency; ≥ 3 unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks. B: At or before 34 weeks. C: Three or more. D: At or beyond 10 weeks. E: Anatomic causes must be excluded.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had three consecutive miscarriages at 7, 8 and 9 weeks. Uterine imaging, hormones and both parents' karyotypes are normal. Anticardiolipin IgG is high on two tests 8 weeks apart. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks is a clinical criterion; aCL in medium or high titer twice ≥ 6 weeks apart is a lab criterion. APS = 1 clinical + 1 lab. A: Not tested; aCL explains it. C: Not tested; aCL explains it. D: Not tested; aCL explains it. E: Not tested; aCL explains it.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman had an ischemic stroke. Anticardiolipin IgM is high at diagnosis and again 3 weeks later. What is still needed to diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome?

options.A: A positive lupus anticoagulant as well
options.C: A repeat test 6 or more weeks later

questions.explanation: The lab criterion needs aCL (IgG and/or IgM, medium or high titer) on ≥ 2 occasions ≥ 6 weeks apart. Her stroke meets the clinical criterion. A: One lab criterion is enough. B: One event is enough. D: APS can be primary. E: At least 6 weeks apart.

questions.stem: A woman has a positive lupus anticoagulant on two tests 8 weeks apart but has never had a thrombosis or pregnancy loss. How is she classified?
questions.explanation: APS = 1 clinical criterion + 1 laboratory criterion. Antibodies alone are not the syndrome. A: Needs a clinical criterion. B: Needs a clinical criterion and lupus. C: Not a category. E: Antibodies are acquired.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a DVT has a prolonged aPTT that does not correct on 1:1 mixing but shortens with excess phospholipid. A factor VIII inhibitor and heparin are excluded. What is present?
questions.explanation: LA: prolonged phospholipid-dependent test, no correction on mixing with normal platelet-poor plasma, shortening with excess phospholipid, other coagulopathies excluded. A: Excluded. B: Would correct on mixing. C: Excluded. D: Would correct on mixing.

questions.stem: A patient's prolonged aPTT corrects on mixing with normal plasma. What is the next step in a lupus anticoagulant work-up?

options.D: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: Mix corrects → incubated mixing study: no correction → phospholipid dependence; correction → factor assays. A: Done when the mix does not correct. C: Stop when both screening tests are normal. D: Done when the aPTT is normal. E: Not the next step.

questions.stem: A prolonged aPTT corrects on mixing and also on an incubated mix. What comes next?

options.B: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: A mix that corrects (also after incubation) points to a factor deficiency: factor assays identify it. A: For a mix that does not correct. B: A screening test. C: Correction points away from an inhibitor. D: Already done.

questions.stem: In a lupus anticoagulant work-up the aPTT is normal. What is the next step?

options.C: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: Test 1 (aPTT) normal → test 2 (dRVVT); if both normal, stop. A: For an abnormal screening test. B: Later in the algorithm. D: Only if test 2 is also normal. E: After a mix that does not correct.

questions.stem: Each is a screening test for lupus anticoagulant EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Screening tests: aPTT, kaolin clotting time, dilute Russell's viper venom time, dilute PT, Textarin time. A: Screening test. B: Screening test. C: Screening test. E: Screening test.

questions.stem: Before a lupus anticoagulant is confirmed, which condition must be excluded?
questions.explanation: The last step is to exclude other coagulopathies, such as a factor VIII inhibitor or heparin. B: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. C: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. D: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. E: Does not prolong the aPTT this way.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman presents with syncope. She had coronary stents at 31 and a pulmonary embolism at 33. Now she has bilateral leg DVTs, a pulmonary embolism, and a cool right foot with absent distal pulses. Which abnormality best explains both her arterial and venous clots?
questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant and hyperhomocysteinemia cause arterial and venous thrombosis; FVL, G20210A and the deficiencies cause venous thrombosis. A: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous. E: Venous.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man had a myocardial infarction last year and now has a DVT. Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin tests are negative twice. Which abnormality best explains both events?
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia and lupus anticoagulant cause arterial and venous thrombosis. With LA excluded, hyperhomocysteinemia remains. B: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous. E: Venous.

questions.stem: Each causes venous but not arterial thrombosis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia (and lupus anticoagulant) cause arterial and venous thrombosis. A: Venous. B: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous.

questions.stem: Among patients with venous thrombosis, which defect is found most often?

options.E: Antithrombin, protein C or S deficiency

questions.explanation: In venous thrombosis: FVL 12–40%, hyperhomocysteinemia 10–20%, APS 10–20%, G20210A 6–18%, antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency 5–15%. A: 6–18%. B: 10–20%. D: 10–20%. E: 5–15%.

questions.stem: What share of patients with venous thrombosis carry prothrombin G20210A?
questions.explanation: Prothrombin G20210A is found in 6–18% of patients with venous thrombosis. A: Factor V Leiden. B: Hyperhomocysteinemia or APS. C: Antithrombin, protein C and S deficiencies. E: FVL among inherited thrombophilias.

questions.stem: Each is a reason to test for thrombophilia EXCEPT:

options.C: A first DVT after surgery at 70
options.E: A sister with a PE at age 30

questions.explanation: Work-up: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of clots at a young age. Testing is usually not the answer. A: Young age. B: Unusual location. D: Listed. E: Family history at a young age.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has a first DVT after a long-haul flight. His brother had a pulmonary embolism at 30 and his father a DVT at 35. Which feature most supports a thrombophilia work-up?
questions.explanation: Indications: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of venous or arterial clots at a young age. A: A provoking factor, not an indication. C: A leg DVT is a usual site. D: This is his first. E: Not an indication.

questions.stem: In the 43-year-old woman with syncope, coronary stents at 31 and two PEs, which feature most supports a thrombophilia work-up?

options.A: A family history of breast cancer
options.E: Repeated thrombosis at a young age

questions.explanation: Indications: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of clots at a young age. A: Not an indication. B: A risk factor, not an indication. C: Not an indication. D: Not an indication.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman of Chinese descent has a right leg DVT at 30 weeks of her first pregnancy. She took oral contraceptives for years. Family and medical history are noncontributory; CBC, PT and aPTT are normal. Which test is most appropriate before anticoagulation?

options.B: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene analysis
options.D: Protein C, protein S and antithrombin levels

questions.explanation: Her DVT has a clear trigger (pregnancy; estrogen exposure is a listed acquired risk factor), the site is usual, it is her first event, and there is no family history of clots. The slides give no answer key; this follows the work-up slide: thrombophilia testing is usually not the answer. B: A provoked first clot; testing is usually not the answer. C: No other APS feature. D: Not indicated for a provoked clot. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer develops a DVT while still walking normally. Which arm of Virchow's triad does his cancer mainly add?
questions.explanation: Malignancy is an acquired thrombophilia: a hypercoagulable state, the "abnormal blood" arm of Virchow's triad. A: He is mobile; the cancer acts on the blood. B: Not the main effect. C: Not an arm of the triad. E: Not an arm of the triad.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had two DVTs. Protein C activity is normal, but activated protein C works poorly because its cofactor is low. Which protein is deficient?
questions.explanation: Activated protein C needs protein S to inactivate Va and VIIIa. Hereditary protein S deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia. B: Neutralizes thrombin. C: Activates protein C. D: Contact cofactor. E: Starts coagulation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old on heparin for 6 days develops an arterial thrombosis, and his platelet count has fallen from 250 to 95 × 10⁹/L. Which risk factor for thrombosis is this?
questions.explanation: HIT is an acquired thrombophilia (with APL, MPD, estrogens, malignancy, surgery, immobility). A: Heparin resistance, not a falling platelet count. C: Venous; no platelet fall. D: Venous; no platelet fall. E: No hemolysis is described.
